idiom_name: worker-pool idiom: N goroutines ranging over a shared channel (the runtime already pools OS threads)
implementation_notes: Go has no thread-pool API because the runtime is one: goroutines are multiplexed by an M:N scheduler onto a bounded set of OS threads, GOMAXPROCS bounds parallel execution, and goroutine creation costs far less than an OS thread - so goroutine-per-task is the baseline and no pool is needed to avoid thread churn. The pattern survives in Go as the worker-pool idiom for the cases where concurrency or queue depth must be bounded: start N workers that range over a shared channel (the official pipelines article's fan-out/fan-in), submit with sends, give the channel a buffer to bound the queue, and use sync.WaitGroup or golang.org/x/sync/errgroup to wait. Reach for it to protect a scarce dependency or to bound in-flight work; otherwise plain goroutines plus a semaphore are enough.
code_sketch:
jobs := make(chan Job, 256)
var wg sync.WaitGroup
for i := 0; i < runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0); i++ {
    wg.Add(1)
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); for j := range jobs { handle(j) } }()
}
for _, j := range source() { jobs <- j }   // blocks while the buffer is full
close(jobs)
wg.Wait()
pitfalls: Exactly one goroutine closes the jobs channel, and only after the last send: sending on a closed channel panics, and closing twice panics.
A blocked producer waiting for a full channel while workers wait for that same producer's next value deadlocks; size the buffer for the producer's capacity or select on ctx.Done().
Workers ranging over a channel that is never closed leak forever, and an unrecovered panic in any worker kills the whole process.
